prerequisites: Describe a comparison while keeping exposure time and other conditions the same.
goals: Distinguish an energy store from a transfer pathway.
Explain infrared heating using surface absorption and energy transfer.
Recognise the limits of a simple black-versus-white comparison.
Apply conservation of energy and calculate efficiency, work, kinetic energy, gravitational potential energy and power.
Explain thermal transfer and compare insulation investigations.
Trace electricity-generation pathways and compare resources (4.18P–4.19P: Paper 2 only).

sections.title: Energy stores and transfer pathways
paragraphs: An energy store describes where energy is associated with a system. The specification names chemical, kinetic, gravitational, elastic, thermal, magnetic, electrostatic and nuclear stores. A transfer describes how energy moves between systems: mechanically, electrically, by heating or by radiation. Avoid describing heat as a substance stored inside an object.

In an electric infrared heater, energy is supplied electrically to the heating element. The hot element emits electromagnetic radiation. When another surface absorbs some of that radiation, energy enters its thermal store. Infrared can travel through a vacuum; no stream of warm air between heater and surface is required.

Conduction transfers energy through interactions between neighbouring particles, with mobile electrons also important in metals. Convection transfers energy by the bulk movement of a fluid. These mechanisms can occur alongside radiation, so identify the mechanism asked about rather than assuming there is only one transfer in an actual room.

example.question: A lamp heats a metal panel across an air gap. Describe the energy transfer to the panel.
steps: The powered lamp emits infrared radiation.
The panel absorbs some incident radiation.
Its thermal store increases and it usually warms.
example.explanation: Radiation is the transfer pathway; thermal is the store. An air gap does not mean heating must occur by convection.

practice.question: Could the same radiation transfer occur across a vacuum gap?
practice.answer: Yes. Electromagnetic radiation needs no material medium.
practice.explanation: Conduction and convection need matter, whereas infrared radiation can propagate through empty space.

sections.title: Why surfaces absorb infrared differently
paragraphs: In the usual IGCSE comparison, a dull black surface is a better absorber and emitter of thermal radiation than a light or shiny surface under comparable conditions. A shiny surface is a poor absorber and a good reflector. Real surfaces have wavelength-dependent properties; visible colour alone does not precisely determine every material's infrared behaviour.

Under the same incident infrared intensity and over the same time, the better absorber receives more energy. If the objects have the same mass, material and relevant heat losses, the better absorber warms faster. Keep those conditions explicit: a colour comparison alone cannot determine the exact temperature change of two different objects.

For the paint-heating observation, explain a chain: the black coating absorbs infrared more effectively, so more energy is transferred to it in the same time, helping the paint harden sooner. A reverse explanation using the white coating is equally clear. Greater emission is a cooling pathway and does not, by itself, explain faster warming under an external lamp.

An object both emits and absorbs radiation. Net warming depends on incoming and outgoing energy together. A good absorber can also be a good emitter; those properties are compatible. Surface temperature matters too, so do not claim that a cooler black object must emit more than every hotter light-coloured object.

For the same surface area and finish, a hotter object emits thermal radiation at a greater rate. Net transfer also depends on radiation absorbed from the surroundings. At thermal equilibrium, absorption and emission continue but balance; constant temperature does not mean neither process occurs.

example.question: Two identical panels receive 120 J of infrared energy each. One absorbs 90 J and the other 30 J. Compare energy transferred into the panels by absorption.
steps: The first panel absorbs 90 J; the second absorbs 30 J.
The first receives 60 J more by absorption.
Its absorbed energy is three times as large.
example.explanation: These invented figures illustrate absorption, not a universal percentage for black or white paint. Heat losses would also be needed to predict net warming.

practice.question: A student says a black panel heats faster because it emits more infrared. Improve the explanation.
practice.answer: Under equal incident radiation, the black panel is the better absorber, so it receives more energy in the same time.
practice.explanation: Emission removes energy from the panel. The explanation needs absorption of energy from the heater.

steps: Identify which surface absorbs more of the incident infrared.
Link this to greater energy transfer during equal exposure.
Connect that transfer to the observed faster warming or hardening.
answerGuide.caution: State the two physical ideas clearly. They can appear in one sentence; do not invent a requirement for two separate sentences. Keep absorption distinct from emission.

commonMistakes: Treating absorption and emission as synonyms.
Predicting exact temperature changes from surface colour without mass, material and heat-loss information.

sections.title: Energy, force and power units
paragraphs: Use kilograms for mass, metres for distance or height, metres per second for speed, metres per second squared for acceleration, newtons for force, seconds for time, joules for energy or work, and watts for power. A joule is equivalent to one newton metre; one watt means one joule transferred each second.

Convert quantities before substitution: 250 g = 0.250 kg, 80 cm = 0.80 m and 2 minutes = 120 s. A kilowatt is 1000 W. Energy and power are different quantities: a power rating describes a transfer rate, so energy also depends on operating time.

example.question: A motor transfers 900 J in 0.5 minutes. Convert the time and calculate its average power.
example.explanation: Dividing by 0.5 without converting minutes gives a value in J/min, not watts.

commonMistakes: Using grams in an equation requiring kilograms.
Calling a joule a unit of power.

sections.title: Conservation, efficiency and Sankey diagrams
paragraphs: Energy is conserved: it cannot be created or destroyed. Define the system and follow transfers across its boundary. In a steady device with no accumulating store, total energy supplied equals all energy outputs. Energy described as wasted still exists; it is less useful for the chosen purpose, often dispersed into the surroundings' thermal stores.

Efficiency = useful energy output / total energy output × 100%. For a steady device over the same time interval, total output equals input, so the input can be used as the denominator. Decide what useful means: heating is useful for a heater but usually unwanted from a motor.

In a Sankey diagram, arrow width is proportional to energy. Incoming width must equal the combined outgoing widths when energy is not accumulating. A broad outgoing arrow is a large transfer, not necessarily a useful one. Label quantities and the purpose of the device.

example.question: A motor receives 500 J. It transfers 300 J mechanically to a load and the rest by heating. Find the unwanted transfer and efficiency.
steps: Energy conserved: unwanted transfer = 500 − 300 = 200 J.
A Sankey drawn at 1 mm per 10 J has input width 50 mm, useful width 30 mm and unwanted width 20 mm.
example.explanation: Use total energy in the denominator. Dividing by only the wasted energy is not efficiency.

diagram.alt: Motor Sankey: 500 joules supplied splits into 300 joules of useful mechanical transfer and 200 joules of unwanted heating; widths in ratio five to three to two.
diagram.caption: Arrow widths show the energy balance for this motor. The 200 J is transferred to surroundings, not destroyed.

practice.question: A lamp receives 800 J and transfers 120 J as useful light. Find its efficiency and unwanted output.
practice.explanation: 120/800 × 100 = 15; 800 − 120 = 680. Useful and unwanted outputs add to the input.

sections.title: Conduction and convection
paragraphs: In a solid, particles near a hotter region have more random kinetic energy and transfer energy to neighbours by interactions. The particles vibrate about their positions; they do not flow from the hot end to the cold end. Mobile electrons also transfer energy in metals, making metals effective thermal conductors.

Convection involves bulk movement of a fluid: a liquid or gas. A heated region usually expands and becomes less dense than the surrounding cooler fluid. It rises under the resulting buoyant effect; cooler, denser fluid moves in to replace it. Continued heating and cooling can maintain circulation.

A heater near the floor warms nearby air. The warmer air rises and cooler air moves towards the heater, helping transfer energy around the room. A convection current does not occur inside a rigid solid. Say that warm fluid rises, rather than that heat itself rises: energy can transfer downwards by conduction or radiation.

In a room, air warmed beside a heater can expand, become less dense and rise. Cooler, denser air moves in below to replace it, creating circulation. Near a cold window, air can cool and descend. The route depends on heater/window position and obstructions; convection is bulk air motion, not a rule that all energy always travels upwards.

example.question: Explain why water heated near the bottom of a beaker can circulate.
steps: Water near the heat source warms, expands and becomes less dense.
This warmer water rises while cooler, denser water moves down to replace it.
The moving water carries energy, forming a convection current.
example.explanation: Link temperature to density and density to movement. Saying only 'hot water rises' leaves out the cause.

commonMistakes: Saying heated particles become individually larger.
Describing convection in a metal rod.

sections.title: Reducing unwanted transfers
paragraphs: Match each insulation feature to a transfer mechanism. Fibres or foam trap small pockets of air: air is a poor conductor and small enclosed pockets limit bulk convection. Thick loft insulation reduces unwanted energy transfer through a roof.

Double glazing uses two panes and a narrow enclosed gas gap. The gas conducts poorly and the narrow gap limits convection; it is not generally a vacuum. Draught proofing reduces the exchange of warmed indoor air with cooler outdoor air.

A vacuum flask uses a vacuum between its walls to prevent conduction and convection across that gap. Shiny facing surfaces reduce radiation across the gap. A stopper reduces transfer through the opening; conduction through supports and the stopper means the flask is not perfectly insulated.

example.question: Why does a vacuum alone not make a flask a perfect insulator?
steps: A vacuum blocks conduction and convection across the gap.
Radiation can cross a vacuum.
There can also be conduction through the stopper and supports.
example.explanation: Identify the remaining pathways instead of treating a vacuum as a barrier to all energy transfer.

sections.title: Investigating conduction
paragraphs: Compare equal-sized rods of different materials heated in the same way. Measure temperature at the same distance from the heated end after equal times. This school comparison indicates thermal response; without controlling heat capacity and losses it is not a precise measurement of thermal conductivity.

Plot temperature at the probe against elapsed time and compare readings at the same times. A larger or earlier rise shows a faster local temperature response in this arrangement. It does not by itself establish how much energy entered the entire rod: mass, specific heat capacity, contact and heat losses also matter.

Conduction transfers energy through interactions in the rod without the solid travelling to the probe. In metals, mobile electrons contribute. Repeated readings and the same geometry/probe contact help separate a consistent response from an accidental contact difference.

apparatus: Equal-length, equal-diameter rods of different materials
Controlled hot-water bath, clamps, temperature probes, ruler and timer
method: Clamp the rods with equal lengths immersed in the bath; attach probes at equal distances from the waterline.
Record initial temperatures, heat using the same bath conditions, and record temperature at fixed time intervals.
Repeat from the same starting temperature and compare temperature-time patterns.
variables: Measure temperature at a fixed position over time.
Control dimensions, immersion depth, probe position, starting temperature and bath temperature.
safety: Use teacher supervision for hot water and rods; clamp securely and allow cooling before handling.
quality: Ensure the probes make equivalent thermal contact.
Repeat measurements and report scatter; do not infer conductivity from a single unreplicated reading.

commonMistakes: Comparing rods of different thickness without accounting for geometry.
Treating the time to warm as a measurement of heat alone.

example.question: Original assumed readings: two same-sized rods start at 22°C. After the same heating interval, the probes read 34°C for A and 29°C for B. What does this establish?
steps: A rises 34 − 22 = 12°C; B rises 29 − 22 = 7°C.
A has the greater local temperature rise under these conditions.
Do not report an exact conductivity or energy ratio from this transient comparison; heat capacity, contact and losses remain relevant.
example.explanation: The readings support a measured temperature response, with a limited inference about material heat transfer. They are invented examples, not results of a performed experiment.

practice.question: Why should the probes be attached at the same distance from the heated end?
practice.answer: Probe position changes the route length and local temperature response. Unequal distances would confound the material comparison.
practice.explanation: State how a control affects the measurement, rather than listing controls without a reason.

sections.title: Seeing a convection current
paragraphs: A small amount of visible dye can trace water movement. Heating gently near one lower side of a water-filled vessel can reveal a rising coloured stream and a return flow away from the heat source. The dye is a tracer: its motion shows water movement rather than displaying energy itself.

In the ordinary warm-water conditions of this school demonstration, locally heated water expands and becomes less dense than surrounding cooler water. Buoyancy makes that warmer fluid rise; cooler water moves in, allowing a circulating current while the temperature difference is maintained.

The unheated comparison helps distinguish circulation associated with heating from diffusion or movement introduced by the pipette. Use a small tracer addition without stirring, record the observed path and avoid treating every coloured movement as proof that heating caused it. These instructions describe a proposed investigation, not a performed observation.

apparatus: Teacher-approved tracer dye, pipette, supported low-power heat source
method: Let the water settle and introduce a small amount of tracer near the lower heated region without stirring.
Apply gentle local heating and observe the tracer's path from the side.
Record the direction of circulation; repeat after allowing the water to settle.
variables: Change whether local heating is applied.
Observe tracer path rather than treating colour intensity as temperature.
Keep vessel shape, water depth and tracer placement similar.
safety: Use a supported heat-resistant vessel and teacher-supervised heating; avoid boiling or handling hot glass.
Use only the teacher-approved tracer and follow its handling instructions.
quality: Compare with unheated water: spreading by diffusion alone is not evidence of the same bulk circulation.

example.question: In a proposed warmed vessel, a tracer rises beside the lower heater and returns down the cooler side. Explain the expected loop.
steps: Locally warmed water normally expands and becomes less dense under these conditions.
It rises relative to cooler surroundings; cooler water moves to replace it.
Bulk fluid motion transfers energy around the vessel. The tracer follows the water; heat is not a coloured material.
example.explanation: Connect the observation to density and circulation, and compare with an unheated control before attributing movement to heating.

practice.question: Dye spreads slowly in an unheated vessel. Does that alone demonstrate the same heating-driven convection loop?
practice.answer: No. Diffusion or disturbance from adding dye can spread colour without the stated buoyancy-driven loop. Compare direction, circulation and the heating condition.
practice.explanation: Colour movement is evidence to interpret, not a direct display of energy.

sections.title: Comparing radiation absorption
paragraphs: Expose otherwise matched dull-black and shiny surfaces to the same infrared source and compare temperature rise over a fixed time. Keep mass, material and position the same, because these also affect the temperature response. This arrangement compares absorption under external illumination; a cooling experiment instead investigates emission.

Calculate the temperature change from each starting value, then compare equal exposure intervals. Dull-black and shiny finishes can differ in absorption under the stated infrared conditions. A net temperature rise also reflects energy lost by emission, conduction and convection, so it is not a direct measurement of absorptivity.

Keep the radiation source and surfaces specified. Visible colour alone does not establish a surface’s behaviour at every infrared wavelength. Repeating with positions swapped helps detect unequal illumination; a separate cooling comparison is needed to investigate emission rather than conflating the two tests.

apparatus: Matched metal plates with dull-black and shiny finishes
Infrared lamp, two temperature probes, ruler and timer
method: Start the plates at the same temperature and place them at equal distances and orientations to the lamp.
Record both temperatures at equal time intervals during the same exposure.
Repeat from equal starting temperatures, swapping positions to check unequal illumination.
variables: Measure temperature rise over the same interval.
Control plate material, mass, area, probe contact, lamp power, distance and starting temperature.
safety: Avoid looking directly into the lamp; keep skin away from hot plates.
Keep flammable items clear and switch off before repositioning hot equipment.
quality: Compare temperature changes rather than final temperatures alone.
Repeat and swap positions; recognise that conduction, convection and emission also affect net warming.

commonMistakes: Calling a higher starting temperature evidence of better absorption.
Explaining faster heating by greater emission.

example.question: Original assumed matched-plate readings: both start at 20°C. After equal lamp exposure, dull-black reaches 31°C and shiny reaches 26°C. Compare the rises and the conclusion.
steps: Dull-black: 31 − 20 = 11°C; shiny: 26 − 20 = 6°C.
The larger net rise is consistent with greater absorption by the dull-black surface if geometry, material, illumination and other conditions are comparable.
These readings do not give an exact absorption coefficient or show that all losses were radiation.
example.explanation: Invented teaching data illustrate how to compare changes and limit the physical inference; no experiment has been performed.

practice.question: A plate changes 23→29°C and another 19→27°C. Is the higher final temperature enough to claim better absorption?
practice.answer: No. Their rises are 6°C and 8°C, and unequal starting temperatures also make the comparison unfair. Match starting conditions and other controls before drawing the absorption conclusion.
practice.explanation: Subtract each starting value and identify the confound; neither final temperature nor these unmatched changes isolate absorptivity.

sections.title: Work done by a force
paragraphs: Work done is energy transferred by a force. For a constant force acting along the displacement, W = F × d. Use force in newtons and distance moved in the direction of that force in metres, giving work in joules.

Identify the force whose work is requested. For a load pulled at constant speed against resistance, the pulling force transfers energy even though the resultant force and change in kinetic energy are zero. If there is no displacement, the work on the object by that force is zero in this model.

example.question: A 35 N horizontal force pulls a crate 4.0 m in its direction. Calculate the work done.
steps: W = F × d.
example.explanation: The relevant distance is along the force. Work is an energy transfer, not a force.

practice.question: A constant force transfers 180 J while moving an object 6.0 m along its direction. Find the force.

sections.title: Kinetic and gravitational potential energy
paragraphs: Near Earth's surface, the increase in gravitational potential energy is m × g × h, where h is the vertical rise, mass is in kg and g is in N/kg. State or use the supplied value of g. Potential energy is measured relative to a chosen level; the change is what matters.

Kinetic energy = ½ × m × v². Square the speed, not the mass and not the entire product. Doubling speed at fixed mass gives four times the kinetic energy; doubling mass at fixed speed gives twice the kinetic energy.

example.question: A 2.0 kg trolley moves at 3.0 m/s and is then raised by 0.80 m. Calculate its initial kinetic energy and the gain in gravitational potential energy, using g = 10 N/kg.
steps: Initial KE = ½ × 2.0 × 3.0² = 9.0 J.
example.explanation: These are two separate calculations. They do not imply the initial motion alone can lift the trolley that high.

practice.question: A 0.50 kg object has 16 J of kinetic energy. Find its speed.

sections.title: Linking energy stores and motion
paragraphs: When a falling object starts from rest and resistance is negligible, the decrease in gravitational potential energy equals the increase in kinetic energy: mgh = ½mv². The mass cancels, giving v² = 2gh under those assumptions.

If resistance acts, some energy is transferred to thermal stores, so the kinetic-energy gain is smaller. Write a balance that includes these transfers instead of setting all lost gravitational potential energy equal to kinetic energy. For a rising object or an externally driven system, also include its initial stores and any energy supplied by forces.

example.question: A 1.0 kg object falls from rest through 5.0 m. During the fall 18 J is transferred to thermal stores. Find its speed, using g = 10 N/kg.
steps: Decrease in GPE = 1.0 × 10 × 5.0 = 50 J.
Gain in KE = 50 − 18 = 32 J.
example.explanation: The resistance transfer is included before solving for speed. Ignoring it would predict too high a speed.

commonMistakes: Cancelling the mass before checking every term in the balance.
Using height travelled along a slope instead of the vertical change.

sections.title: Power is a transfer rate
paragraphs: Power is the rate of energy transfer or work done. Average power = energy transferred / time taken = W/t. A higher-power device transfers more energy in the same time, or the same energy in less time.

Use seconds for time and joules for work to obtain watts. Rearrange to W = Pt or t = W/P as required. Be clear whether a power value is the total input or useful output: an inefficient motor's useful lifting power is below its electrical input power.

example.question: A motor raises a 12 kg load vertically by 2.0 m in 3.0 s. Find its average useful power, using g = 10 N/kg.
steps: Useful work = mgh = 12 × 10 × 2.0 = 240 J.
Useful power = 240/3.0 = 80 W.
example.explanation: 80 W is useful output power; input power would require efficiency information.

practice.question: A 250 W device transfers energy steadily for 40 s. How much does it transfer?

sections.title: Electricity generation · Paper 2 only
paragraphs: Wind transfers energy from moving air mechanically to a turbine, which drives a generator. In hydroelectric generation, water loses gravitational potential energy as it moves to a lower level and drives turbines. Tidal flow and water waves can also transfer energy mechanically to generating equipment; the details of the machinery differ.

In a fossil-fuel station, burning fuel transfers energy from its chemical store by heating water and producing steam. Steam drives a turbine connected to a generator. In a nuclear station, fission releases energy from nuclear stores to heat a working fluid; fuel is not burned in a chemical combustion reaction.

Geothermal resources use energy from hot underground rock or fluid. Where conditions allow electricity generation, hot fluid or steam drives a turbine-generator system. Do not describe geothermal as energy created by the generator.

Solar heating systems absorb radiation to warm a fluid. A domestic solar water heater supplies thermal energy directly and does not by itself generate electricity; a solar thermal power station can use a heated fluid to drive a turbine-generator. Solar cells instead transfer energy from radiation electrically, without a turbine.

example.question: Explain the difference between a solar cell and a solar water-heating panel.
steps: Both absorb energy from solar radiation.
A solar cell supplies energy electrically.
A water-heating panel transfers energy to the thermal store of water; electricity generation would need additional equipment.
example.explanation: Solar cell and solar heater are different technologies, even though both use sunlight.

sections.title: Comparing electricity resources · Paper 2 only
paragraphs: Renewable resources are replenished on a human timescale. Wind, moving water, solar and geothermal resources can be renewable; fossil fuels and uranium are finite fuel resources. Renewable does not mean continuously available or environmentally impact-free.

Wind and solar have no fuel combustion during operation, but output depends on conditions. A supply system may need storage, other generators or interconnection when output is low. Tidal timing is predictable but output varies over the tidal cycle. Reservoir hydroelectricity can respond rapidly but depends on stored water and suitable geography; dams may flood habitats.

Fossil-fuel generation can supply controllable output but releases carbon dioxide during combustion and can release other pollutants. Nuclear generation has low operational carbon dioxide emissions and can provide sustained output, but radioactive waste, construction costs and decommissioning require management. Neither technology should be described as having no environmental cost.

Geothermal output can be steady at suitable sites, but appropriate geology and drilling limit deployment. In comparisons, connect a stated advantage or disadvantage to the location and supply need. Distinguish operational emissions from emissions associated with manufacture, construction and fuel supply.

practice.question: A sunny region wants to rely entirely on solar cells. Give a supply limitation and a way to address it.
practice.answer: Output falls at night and can fall in cloudy conditions. Storage or another supply source can provide energy during low-output periods.
practice.explanation: Being renewable does not make solar output constant. A response should connect variability to a practical supply measure.

sections.title: Following energy through a system
paragraphs: Start by choosing the system and identifying the store that decreases. In a battery-powered torch, the battery’s chemical store decreases as energy is transferred electrically to the lamp. The lamp transfers energy by light and heating; the surroundings’ thermal stores increase. Electrical transfer is a pathway, not a store named in this specification.

As a trolley rolls downhill, the gravitational store of the Earth–trolley system decreases. The trolley’s kinetic store increases if it speeds up, while friction can also increase thermal stores. Stretching a spring transfers energy mechanically into its elastic store; release can transfer energy mechanically to a moving toy.

Work is needed to push two like magnetic poles closer together. Energy is stored in their magnetic interaction; releasing them can increase their kinetic stores as they move apart. Similarly, work done bringing two like electric charges closer increases the electrostatic store of the system. The interaction involves both objects, so name the system rather than claiming a force itself is a store.

A hot cup has a thermal store. It transfers energy to cooler surroundings by heating and radiation as it cools. In nuclear fission, energy released from the nuclear store can increase the thermal store of a reactor’s working fluid. The fuel is not undergoing chemical combustion.

The specification groups emitted light and sound as radiation transfer examples. Light can carry energy through a vacuum; sound carries energy through vibrations in a material medium and cannot cross a vacuum. The shared transfer label does not make sound electromagnetic.

example.question: A spring launches a toy across a rough horizontal floor. Describe the energy changes from release until the toy stops.
steps: During release, the spring’s elastic store decreases as energy is transferred mechanically to the toy.
The toy gains kinetic energy. Some energy may already be transferred to thermal stores and sound during launch.
As the toy slows, its kinetic store decreases while friction transfers energy to thermal stores of the floor, toy and surroundings.
For the complete chosen system, total energy is conserved even though the original store is no longer useful for moving the toy.
example.explanation: Energy is transferred and becomes more spread out; it is not used up or destroyed.

practice.question: A student says a falling object creates kinetic energy. Improve the statement for a fall from rest with negligible air resistance.
practice.answer: Its kinetic energy increases as the gravitational store of the Earth–object system decreases by the same amount.
practice.explanation: The increase is balanced by a decrease in another store; choosing the system makes conservation explicit.

sections.title: Work along a slope and vertical height
paragraphs: Work uses the distance moved in the direction of the force. Gravitational potential energy uses vertical height. For a pull parallel to a slope, these are different distances: use the length travelled along the slope in W = Fd, and the vertical rise in ΔGPE = mgh.

At constant speed the kinetic store is unchanged. Work supplied by a pulling force can still increase gravitational potential energy and overcome friction. Zero resultant work means zero change in kinetic energy; it does not mean every individual force does zero work.

State the model before making the balance. Here the load is rigid, the pull is parallel to a fixed slope, speed is constant, and friction is the only dissipative force. Work supplied = gain in gravitational potential energy + energy transferred by friction.

example.question: A 2.0 kg load is pulled 1.5 m up a slope, rising vertically by 0.60 m. A steady 12 N pull acts parallel to the slope and keeps the speed constant. Use g = 10 N/kg. Find the pulling work, gain in gravitational potential energy and energy transferred by friction.
steps: Pulling work = 12 × 1.5 = 18 J.
Kinetic energy is unchanged because speed is constant.
Energy transferred by friction = 18 − 12 = 6.0 J.
example.explanation: The 18 J input is accounted for by 12 J in gravitational potential energy and 6 J transferred to thermal stores. Using 0.60 m in the pulling-work calculation mixes two different distances.

practice.question: For the same 2.0 kg load and slope, neglect friction. What constant pull parallel to the slope would keep the speed constant?
practice.answer: Required work = 12 J, so F = 12/1.5 = 8.0 N.
practice.explanation: The pull supplies the gravitational energy gain only. This is less than the 12 N required in the frictional example.

commonMistakes: Do not put the distance along the slope into mgh.
Constant speed does not mean no energy transfer.
Do not set useful output equal to total supplied work when energy is dissipated.
